questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Academic opportunity was the biggest aspect, having worked with French thinkers and writers throughout my degree. The language aspect, then, was probably the most important of all. A personal connection with the Sorbonne was also present, with my father and grandmother both having spent time there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In true French grading fashion, there is always room for improvement.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Sorbonne certainly doesn't make it easy if you want to be well ahead of time. But upon arrival the faculty had distributed pamphlets by email, clearly explaining the process, when to arrive for the orientations and how to choose courses.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Introductory orientations, as well as the possibility of meeting with an Erasmus coordinator specific to my study area within her office hours.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is difficult in Paris. I recommend Facebook groups, acquaintances, and to be vigilant. Don't hesitate to take interest.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is, I think, a good way to have an experience of living in the city, not just venturing out into it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can't comment. There is the Cité Universitaire in Paris, and I have heard both good and bad.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Sorbonne is old school, and you register by crosschecking course lists and timetables. These documents are difficult to find if you don't know where to look. A link was distributed, but much later than expected. It is understandable, there is a lot of organising to fit all the courses in at logical times. At the beginning of the year you meet in person, having prepared your courses, and fill them in on a piece of paper, which is then handed to your coordinator. (S)he handles the rest.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus orientation pamphlet distributed by mail and the coordinator. Ask people who have been on an exchange before!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: More or less successful, all in all.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress too much about it. Keep a level head, it's gonna work itself out.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was high. Studying literature in French on master level at the Sorbonne is no walk in the park. There is loads to read. Having said that, some of the students at the Sorbonne are very young, and do not necessarily have the same base of knowledge. I was surprised by the very introductory nature of one of my courses, it being a master seminar.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching at UCPH is a lot more interactive, the students taking part in discussions, sometimes even in shaping the curriculum. At the Sorbonne, with few exceptions, you show up, listen to a lecture for two hours, then exit. There is always the possibility of posing questions, but the style is a lot more conservative generally. But the academic level is high all around.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Take a language course or two to lessen the workload. The system is badly designed for master exchange. I had to take 5 master seminars, each with their written assignment exam, whereas the French students only have 2.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: No unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I expected Paris to be expensive and it was. The fresh food markets were cheaper than the supermarkets, I would recommend using them for grocery shopping.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had enough activities outside university so I cannot comment as I did not particularly partake in the University organised activities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are some clubs and sports associations. The opportunity is there, it seems. Again, I am not the right person to answer this.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do sports to compensate for all the cerebral work! And visit as many museums as you can. There are loads. If the city feels too crowded, take the train to the Fontainebleau forest.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Take a trip to the rest of France as well, like Bretagne, Normandie, Provence …

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It suits me well, they are generally outgoing, polite and forthcoming.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to them! They are friendly!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The French are very polite, and might seem impersonal at first, but if you talk to them they are (mostly) very approachable and ready for a chat.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The talkativeness, and the fact that people spend a lot of time on the streets. It makes the city very lively and welcoming. Within a week I was on a friendly basis with the staff at the restaurant on the corner of my building.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Keep calm. It's stressful, but it will work itself out.
Find something to do, an activity, outside of the University. That way you'll meet more and different people.
Talk to people and don't hold back. You'll most likely be gone in a few months, there is really everything to win by getting a little out of your comfort zone.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't expect them to do you any favours. You need to be organised and decide for yourself. Ask someone to put you in a group chat with the normal students, you'll have access to insight and info which is hard to come by otherwise.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Too much to describe. But the language, and the people I got to know.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The exam period was the most challenging, stressful and difficult academic period of my life, and it was equally as rewarding to overcome.
